comply-in.span: Semantic and keyword search, used for what each actually excels at—meaning understanding vs. exact matching.
A specific search strategy, with the reasoning behind it, before any implementation begins.
Combining vector embeddings with BM25 or TF-IDF in a single query, the standard 2026 pattern for robust retrieval.
If your use case doesn't need the complexity of semantic search, I'll say so—and recommend keyword search instead.

sec-head.h2: What is Semantic Search? What is Keyword Search?

p: Semantic search uses vector embeddings and neural models to understand the meaning behind a query, matching conceptually related content even when no exact words match. Keyword search relies on exact term matching via algorithms like BM25 or TF-IDF, delivering fast, precise results when the query terms appear in the document. Both are fundamental retrieval methods, and the real decision comes down to whether your hardest problem is understanding intent or catching exact phrases—and hybrid search combines them for the best of both worlds.

sec-head.h2: Search comparison: Semantic Search vs Keyword Search

td: Understands meaning, synonyms, and context via embeddings
Fast exact match on literal terms and metadata
Content discovery, Q&A, chatbots, long-tail queries
E-commerce, product catalogs, structured fields, known IDs
Requires embedding model, vector database, and reindexing pipeline
Simple inverted index with TF-IDF or BM25; low overhead
Higher due to embedding generation and ANN search (20–50ms typical)
Low (5–10ms) for direct index lookup and scoring
Handles synonyms, paraphrases, and misspellings naturally
Fails on misspelled or out-of-vocabulary terms unless fuzzy logic is added
May miss literal terms if embedding drifts or vectors are misaligned
Perfect for exact product codes, names, and boolean filters

p: Most production retrieval systems use both together: semantic search for understanding broad intent, and keyword search for precision on exact terms. This is the standard architecture I build when a project genuinely needs both recall and relevance—and it's the foundation of Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) in 2026.
